sources.note: Step 82: variance/interval propagation of uncertainty through the Observation->Evidence->Knowledge->Model->Prediction->Decision pipeline; covers linear/nonlinear (delta method) propagation, correlation, Bayesian updating, confidence-vs-probability, calibration, decision sensitivity/robustness, aleatory-vs-epistemic and parameter-vs-model uncertainty, uncertainty budgets, and uncertainty-impact propagation graphs.

rows.anchor: We now test whether our mathematical model remains correct when uncertainty passes through multiple layers ... Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision. Uncertainty must propagate through reasoning; it must never disappear merely because the representation changed.
rows.statement: States the step's central principle: uncertainty must propagate through the reasoning pipeline (Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision) and must never disappear merely because representation changed.

rows.anchor: 82.1 — Measurement uncertainty ... X=100 with σ_X=5. We should not represent the epistemic state simply as X=100. A better representation is X≈100±5 under an explicitly defined uncertainty model.
rows.statement: Argues a measured quantity with known measurement uncertainty (X=100, σ_X=5) should be represented as X≈100±5 under an explicit uncertainty model, not as a bare point value.

rows.anchor: 82.2 — Experiment 1: uncertainty deletion ... X=100±5. Y=X+10. System stores Y=110. Expected: UncertaintyLossDetected. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a system that computes Y=X+10 from X=100±5 and stores only Y=110 (dropping the uncertainty) should trigger UncertaintyLossDetected; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.3 — Simple deterministic transformation ... Y=X+c, then σ_Y=σ_X. 100±5 → 110±5.
rows.statement: For a deterministic shift Y=X+c, uncertainty is unchanged: σ_Y=σ_X, e.g. 100±5 → 110±5.

rows.anchor: 82.4 — Experiment 2 ... X=100±5, Y=X+10. Expected: Y=110±5. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2 confirms the additive-shift rule: X=100±5, Y=X+10 yields Y=110±5; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.5 — Multiplication ... Y=aX where a is exact. σ_Y=|a|σ_X. X=100±5, a=2 → Y=200±10.
rows.statement: For Y=aX with exact scalar a, σ_Y=|a|σ_X; e.g. X=100±5 scaled by a=2 gives Y=200±10.

rows.anchor: 82.6 — Experiment 3 ... Expected: σ_Y=10. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3 confirms the multiplicative scaling rule numerically: σ_Y=10; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.7 — Addition of independent uncertainties ... Z=X+Y. If X,Y independent: Var(Z)=Var(X)+Var(Y). σ_Z=sqrt(σ_X^2+σ_Y^2).
rows.statement: For independent X,Y summed as Z=X+Y, variances add: Var(Z)=Var(X)+Var(Y), so σ_Z=sqrt(σ_X²+σ_Y²).

rows.anchor: 82.8 — Experiment 4 ... X=100±3, Y=50±4. Z=150, σ_Z=sqrt(3²+4²)=5. Expected: Z=150±5. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4 confirms independent-variance addition numerically: X=100±3 plus Y=50±4 gives Z=150±5; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.9 — Correlation changes everything ... Cov(X,Y)≠0. Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independence cannot be assumed automatically. This connects directly to our previous evidence-independence work.
rows.statement: Warns that when Cov(X,Y)≠0, Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y), so independence cannot be assumed automatically; the file explicitly links this to prior evidence-independence work.

lineage_claims.quote: This connects directly to our previous evidence-independence work.

rows.anchor: 82.10 — Experiment 5 ... System assumes Cov(X,Y)=0. But both measurements originate from the same sensor. Expected: PotentialUnderestimatedUncertainty. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: assuming independence (Cov=0) for two measurements from the same sensor is expected to yield PotentialUnderestimatedUncertainty; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.11 — Negative correlation ... If Cov(X,Y)<0, uncertainty can partially cancel. Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y). Correlation can either increase or decrease uncertainty depending on the transformation.
rows.statement: Shows negative correlation can partially cancel uncertainty in a difference: Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y); correlation's effect on uncertainty is transformation-dependent, not uniformly increasing.

rows.anchor: 82.12 — Experiment 6 ... Two measurement errors are strongly correlated. System assumes independence. Expected: IncorrectVariance. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: assuming independence for strongly correlated measurement errors is expected to produce IncorrectVariance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.13 — Nonlinear transformations ... Y=f(X). Var(Y)≈[f'(E[X])]²Var(X). This is the delta method.
rows.statement: Introduces the delta method: for Y=f(X) with small uncertainty, Var(Y)≈[f'(E[X])]²Var(X).
Worked delta-method example: Y=X² with X=10±1 gives f'(X)=2X so σ_Y≈2(10)(1)=20, i.e. Y≈100±20.

rows.anchor: 82.15 — Experiment 7 ... System calculates 10±1 → 100±1. Expected: FalsePrecision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: a system computing 10±1 → 100±1 (ignoring the delta-method scaling, i.e. treating nonlinear propagation as if uncertainty passes through unchanged) is expected to be FalsePrecision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.16 — Nonlinear uncertainty can be asymmetric ... Y=e^X. A symmetric uncertainty in X produces asymmetric uncertainty in Y. Mean±σ is not universally sufficient.
rows.statement: Argues that strongly nonlinear transforms (e.g. Y=e^X) turn symmetric input uncertainty into asymmetric output uncertainty, so mean±σ is not universally a sufficient representation.

rows.anchor: 82.17 — Experiment 8 ... X=0±2. Y=e^X. System represents Y as 1±2. Expected: InvalidRepresentation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: representing Y=e^X (with X=0±2) as the symmetric interval 1±2 is expected to be InvalidRepresentation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.18 — Distribution-level representation ... For sufficiently complex uncertainty, KnowledgeOS may need P(X) rather than (X,σ). P(Y)=∫P(Y|X)P(X)dX. This is much richer.
rows.statement: Proposes moving from a (mean,σ) representation to a full distribution P(X), with P(Y)=∫P(Y|X)P(X)dX for propagation, as a richer representation.

rows.anchor: 82.19 — Experiment 9 ... Two variables have identical means and variances but their distributions differ significantly. Expected: MeanVarianceRepresentation may not preserve enough information. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: two variables with identical mean and variance but different distribution shapes show that mean/variance representation may not preserve enough information; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.20 — Bayesian updating ... P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E). KnowledgeOS should distinguish Prior from Posterior.
rows.statement: States Bayes' rule P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) and requires KnowledgeOS to distinguish Prior from Posterior explicitly.

rows.anchor: 82.21 — Experiment 10 ... Prior P(H)=0.3. Evidence increases belief to P(H|E)=0.7. System overwrites the prior with 0.7 and loses the evidence relationship. Expected: ProvenanceLoss. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: overwriting a prior (0.3) with the posterior (0.7) and losing the evidence relationship is expected to yield ProvenanceLoss; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.24 — Confidence is not probability ... A confidence score 0.9 does not automatically mean P(H)=0.9. Different uncertainty representations have different semantics. Confidence ≠ Probability.
rows.statement: States as essential that a confidence score (e.g. 0.9) does not automatically equal a probability P(H)=0.9; different uncertainty representations carry different semantics — Confidence ≠ Probability.

rows.anchor: 82.25 — Experiment 12 ... LLM says confidence = 0.95. System stores P(H)=0.95. Expected: SemanticError. Result: PASS. Unless the confidence measure has explicitly been calibrated to represent probability.
rows.statement: Experiment 12: converting an LLM's self-reported confidence=0.95 directly into P(H)=0.95 is a SemanticError unless the confidence measure has been explicitly calibrated to represent probability; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.26 — Calibration ... If a system predicts P(H)=0.8, then among many comparable cases, approximately 80% should be true if the probability is well calibrated. Different from merely asking the model 'how confident are you?'
rows.statement: Defines calibration: a well-calibrated P(H)=0.8 prediction should be true in ~80% of comparable cases empirically, distinct from simply asking a model to self-report confidence.

rows.anchor: 82.27 — Experiment 13 ... AI produces 0.9 confidence. Historical calibration shows only 0.65 of such predictions are correct. Expected: ConfidenceCalibrationProblem. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: an AI's 0.9-confidence predictions being correct only 65% of the time historically is expected to be flagged ConfidenceCalibrationProblem; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.28 — Decision uncertainty ... P(D|E). Often the decision itself is deterministic given the model. D=A if P(H)>0.8 else B. Small changes in P(H) near 0.8 can flip the decision.
rows.statement: Notes that although the decision rule D=A if P(H)>0.8 else B is itself deterministic given the model, small changes in P(H) near the 0.8 threshold can flip the decision.

rows.anchor: 82.29 — Experiment 14 ... P(H)=0.79 → Decision B. New evidence P(H)=0.81 → Decision A. Expected: DecisionSensitivity=True. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: P(H) moving from 0.79 (Decision B) to 0.81 (Decision A) across a 0.8 threshold demonstrates DecisionSensitivity=True; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.30 — Decision boundary ... θ=0.8. P(H)>θ⇒A. Near the boundary |P(H)-θ|≈0, small uncertainty can have large decision impact.
rows.statement: Defines a decision boundary θ=0.8 and argues that near the boundary, small uncertainty in P(H) can have disproportionately large decision impact.

rows.anchor: 82.31 — Experiment 15 ... P(H)=0.801, σ=0.05. System declares DecisionCertain. Expected: FalseCertainty. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: declaring DecisionCertain when P(H)=0.801 has σ=0.05 (uncertainty band straddling the θ=0.8 boundary) is FalseCertainty; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.32 — Probability intervals ... P(H)∈[0.75,0.85]. The decision boundary lies inside the uncertainty interval. Correct status: DecisionUndetermined if the policy requires certainty relative to that boundary.
rows.statement: Proposes representing P(H) as an interval [0.75,0.85]; when the decision boundary θ falls inside this interval, the correct status is DecisionUndetermined (given a policy requiring certainty relative to the boundary).

rows.anchor: 82.33 — Experiment 16 ... P(H)∈[0.75,0.85], θ=0.8. Expected: DecisionStatus=Sensitive/Undetermined. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16 confirms: P(H)∈[0.75,0.85] straddling θ=0.8 yields DecisionStatus=Sensitive/Undetermined; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.34 — Monte Carlo reasoning ... X~P(X). Generate X_1..X_N. D_i=f(X_i). P(D=A)≈(1/N)Σ1[D_i=A]. This can reveal how often a decision changes under plausible uncertainty.
rows.statement: Proposes Monte Carlo simulation (sampling X_i~P(X), computing D_i=f(X_i), estimating P(D=A) by frequency) to reveal how often a decision changes under plausible uncertainty.

type_signature.domain: distribution P(X) x decision function f

rows.anchor: 82.35 — Experiment 17 ... 10,000 plausible simulations produce A: 72%, B: 28%. Expected: KnowledgeOS should be able to represent P(D=A)≈0.72 rather than simply D=A. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations giving A:72%/B:28% should be represented as P(D=A)≈0.72, not collapsed to a bare D=A; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.40 — Epistemic versus aleatory uncertainty ... Aleatory: intrinsic variability X~P(X). Epistemic: lack of knowledge, UnknownParameter. These behave differently.
rows.statement: Distinguishes aleatory uncertainty (intrinsic variability, X~P(X)) from epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge, e.g. an unknown parameter), noting they behave differently.

rows.anchor: 82.41 — Experiment 20 ... System observes varying demand. It labels all uncertainty 'data noise'. But part of the uncertainty comes from missing information about the system. Expected: UncertaintyClassificationError. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: labeling all demand-variation uncertainty as 'data noise' (aleatory) when part is actually epistemic (missing system information) is an UncertaintyClassificationError; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.42 — Why this matters ... If uncertainty is epistemic, MoreEvidence may reduce it. If uncertainty is intrinsic, MoreObservation may not eliminate the underlying variability.
rows.statement: Explains the practical stakes of the aleatory/epistemic distinction: epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by more evidence, while aleatory/intrinsic uncertainty may not be eliminated by more observation.

rows.anchor: 82.43 — Experiment 21 ... Demand is inherently stochastic. Collecting more data does not make tomorrow's demand deterministic. Expected: ResidualAleatoryUncertainty. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: more data collection on inherently stochastic demand cannot eliminate ResidualAleatoryUncertainty; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.44 — Uncertainty budget ... D=f(X_1,...,X_n). Uncertainty(D)=U_1+U_2+... with interaction terms where required. The objective is not merely 'we are uncertain' but 'what is causing the uncertainty?'
rows.statement: Introduces the notion of an uncertainty budget: decomposing Uncertainty(D) for D=f(X_1..X_n) into per-component contributions (plus interaction terms), shifting the question from 'are we uncertain' to 'what is causing the uncertainty'.

rows.anchor: 82.45 — Experiment 22 ... Decision uncertainty is high. Analysis shows 80% comes from one unknown parameter. Expected: ObservationPriority should focus on that parameter. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: an uncertainty budget attributing 80% of decision uncertainty to one parameter implies ObservationPriority should focus there; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.55 — Uncertainty propagation graph ... O_1→K_1→M→P→D. If uncertainty enters at O_1, we should be able to determine which downstream decisions are affected. This is UncertaintyImpactPropagation.
rows.statement: Proposes an uncertainty-propagation/impact graph O_1→K_1→M→P→D enabling determination of which downstream decisions are affected when uncertainty enters at a given observation — named UncertaintyImpactPropagation.

rows.anchor: 82.56 — Experiment 27 ... Observation O_1 is later found unreliable. Expected system identifies K_1 dependent on O_1, then M dependent on K_1, then D dependent on M. Expected: AffectedDecisionSet is discoverable. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: when O_1 is found unreliable, the system must be able to discover the full downstream AffectedDecisionSet (K_1→M→D); result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.57 — This creates a new capability ... Impact(O_i) meaning: which knowledge, models, decisions, policies, or actions depend materially on this observation? This is much stronger than ordinary document search.
rows.statement: Names a new capability Impact(O_i) — determining which knowledge, models, decisions, policies or actions materially depend on a given observation — described as much stronger than ordinary document search.

rows.anchor: 82.58 — Experiment 28 ... A critical source is revoked. System identifies 47 downstream claims and 12 decisions affected. Expected: RevalidationWorkflow. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: revoking a critical source and identifying 47 downstream claims / 12 affected decisions should trigger a RevalidationWorkflow; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.59 — Uncertainty should not silently accumulate ... If the system simply stores Confidence=0.9 at each stage, multiplying 0.9^4 would itself be unjustified. The semantics of the confidence measures must be known.
rows.statement: Warns against naively multiplying stage-wise confidence scores (e.g. 0.9^4 across four pipeline stages) without knowing what each confidence measure actually means semantically.

rows.anchor: 82.60 — Experiment 29 ... System calculates 0.9×0.9×0.9 without defining what each confidence means. Expected: UnsupportedProbabilityCalculation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: multiplying undefined confidence scores (0.9×0.9×0.9) is an UnsupportedProbabilityCalculation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.61 — False precision ... Input: 'roughly 80%' becoming Output: 0.813742. The mathematical formatting has become more precise than the underlying information.
rows.statement: Illustrates false precision: a qualitative input ('roughly 80%') rendered as an overly precise numeric output (0.813742) misrepresents the underlying information's actual precision.

rows.anchor: 82.62 — Experiment 30 ... Source uncertainty is qualitative: 'likely'. System outputs P=0.8734. No calibration exists. Expected: FalsePrecision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: converting a qualitative source ('likely') into an uncalibrated precise number P=0.8734 is FalsePrecision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.63 — Precision versus accuracy ... Precision ≠ Accuracy. A system can produce 0.873421 and still be badly wrong.
rows.statement: States Precision ≠ Accuracy: a highly precise-looking number (0.873421) can still be badly inaccurate.

rows.anchor: 82.64 — Experiment 31 ... Model predicts 87.3421%. Historical calibration shows 52%. Expected: HighNumericalPrecision but LowPredictiveAccuracy. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 31: a model prediction of 87.3421% with historical calibration showing only 52% accuracy demonstrates HighNumericalPrecision but LowPredictiveAccuracy; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.65 — The KnowledgeOS rule ... Representational precision must not exceed epistemically justified precision. This should become a formal design principle.
rows.statement: States the design principle: representational precision must not exceed epistemically justified precision, proposed as a formal KnowledgeOS design principle.

rows.anchor: 82.66 — Decision-level uncertainty state ... enrich True/False/Unknown model. A decision may have Determinate, Sensitive, Underdetermined, Robust depending on the uncertainty structure.
rows.statement: Extends the earlier True/False/Unknown model with decision-level uncertainty states: Determinate, Sensitive, Underdetermined, Robust.

rows.anchor: 82.67 — Experiment 32 ... Decision A wins under 95% of plausible states. Expected: RobustlyA rather than simply A. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 32: a decision that wins in 95% of plausible states should be labeled RobustlyA rather than an unqualified A; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.68 — Decision robustness ... Decision A is robust if ∀u∈U: D(u)=A. This is much stronger than D(E[u])=A.
rows.statement: Defines decision robustness formally: A is robust over uncertainty set U if D(u)=A for all u∈U — much stronger than merely D(E[u])=A (decision at the expected value).

rows.anchor: 82.69 — Experiment 33 ... Expected-value analysis selects A. But for some plausible parameter values, D=B. Expected: A is not robust. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 33: expected-value analysis selecting A while some plausible parameter values give D=B shows A is not robust by the 82.68 definition; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 82.70 — This connects directly to Step 76 ... Decision=f(Knowledge,DecisionModel,Policy). Now: Decision=f(Knowledge,Uncertainty,DecisionModel,Policy,Context). Knowledge itself contains uncertainty.
rows.statement: Enriches Step 76's Decision=f(Knowledge,DecisionModel,Policy) formula to Decision=f(Knowledge,Uncertainty,DecisionModel,Policy,Context), noting Knowledge itself contains uncertainty.

type_signature.domain: Knowledge x Uncertainty x DecisionModel x Policy x Context

lineage_claims.quote: This connects directly to Step 76.

rows.anchor: 82.71 — Full uncertainty-aware pipeline ... Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision with uncertainty U_O→U_K→U_M→U_P→U_D. Every transformation must preserve the semantics of uncertainty.
rows.statement: Restates the full pipeline with a parallel uncertainty-propagation chain U_O→U_K→U_M→U_P→U_D; the requirement is not monotonic increase but that every transformation preserves the semantics of uncertainty.

rows.anchor: 82.72 — New invariants: I_UncertaintyPreservation, I_Dependence, I_ModelUncertainty, I_Calibration, I_EpistemicPrecision, I_DecisionSensitivity, I_UncertaintyImpact
rows.statement: States seven new named invariants: I_UncertaintyPreservation (transformations must not silently discard material uncertainty), I_Dependence (dependencies between uncertain variables must be represented when material), I_ModelUncertainty (model-structure uncertainty must be distinguished from parameter uncertainty), I_Calibration (probabilistic claims should have defined semantics and empirical calibration where applicable), I_EpistemicPrecision (output precision must not misrepresent evidence quality), I_DecisionSensitivity (when uncertainty can change the selected action, sensitivity must remain visible), I_UncertaintyImpact (material upstream evidence changes must permit identification of affected downstream knowledge/decisions).

rows.anchor: 82.73 — Step 82 verdict: STEP 82 — PASS ... KnowledgeOS cannot merely store confidence. It needs a mathematically meaningful uncertainty model and must preserve that uncertainty through transformations. Statistics+Bayesian inference+Causal reasoning+Decision theory+Governance+Software architecture.
rows.statement: Records Step 82 verdict PASS with the conclusion that KnowledgeOS needs a mathematically meaningful uncertainty model preserved through transformations, connecting Statistics, Bayesian inference, Causal reasoning, Decision theory, Governance, and Software architecture.

rows.anchor: Current model after Step 82 ... Reality→Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→CausalModel→Prediction→DecisionModel→Decision→Authority→Action→Outcome→Observation, with three critical cross-cutting structures: Provenance, Uncertainty, Governance. WorldModel≠ValueModel≠PolicyModel≠ExecutionModel.
rows.statement: Presents the cumulative KnowledgeOS pipeline as a closed loop Reality→Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→CausalModel→Prediction→DecisionModel→Decision→Authority→Action→Outcome→Observation, cross-cut by Provenance, Uncertainty and Governance, restating WorldModel≠ValueModel≠PolicyModel≠ExecutionModel.

lexical.anchor: We now test whether our mathematical model remains correct when uncertainty passes through multiple layers ... Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision. Uncertainty must propagate through reasoning; it must never disappear merely because the representation changed.

conceptual.anchor: 82.13 — Nonlinear transformations ... Y=f(X). Var(Y)≈[f'(E[X])]²Var(X). This is the delta method.

formal.anchor: 82.3 — Simple deterministic transformation ... Y=X+c, then σ_Y=σ_X. 100±5 → 110±5.

operational.anchor: 82.2 — Experiment 1: uncertainty deletion ... X=100±5. Y=X+10. System stores Y=110. Expected: UncertaintyLossDetected. Result: PASS

rationale_evidence.anchor: We now test whether our mathematical model remains correct when uncertainty passes through multiple layers ... Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision. Uncertainty must propagate through reasoning; it must never disappear merely because the representation changed.
rationale_evidence.statement: States the step's central principle: uncertainty must propagate through the reasoning pipeline (Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision) and must never disappear merely because representation changed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.1 — Measurement uncertainty ... X=100 with σ_X=5. We should not represent the epistemic state simply as X=100. A better representation is X≈100±5 under an explicitly defined uncertainty model.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues a measured quantity with known measurement uncertainty (X=100, σ_X=5) should be represented as X≈100±5 under an explicit uncertainty model, not as a bare point value.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.11 — Negative correlation ... If Cov(X,Y)<0, uncertainty can partially cancel. Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y). Correlation can either increase or decrease uncertainty depending on the transformation.
rationale_evidence.statement: Shows negative correlation can partially cancel uncertainty in a difference: Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y); correlation's effect on uncertainty is transformation-dependent, not uniformly increasing.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.16 — Nonlinear uncertainty can be asymmetric ... Y=e^X. A symmetric uncertainty in X produces asymmetric uncertainty in Y. Mean±σ is not universally sufficient.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues that strongly nonlinear transforms (e.g. Y=e^X) turn symmetric input uncertainty into asymmetric output uncertainty, so mean±σ is not universally a sufficient representation.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.28 — Decision uncertainty ... P(D|E). Often the decision itself is deterministic given the model. D=A if P(H)>0.8 else B. Small changes in P(H) near 0.8 can flip the decision.
rationale_evidence.statement: Notes that although the decision rule D=A if P(H)>0.8 else B is itself deterministic given the model, small changes in P(H) near the 0.8 threshold can flip the decision.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.30 — Decision boundary ... θ=0.8. P(H)>θ⇒A. Near the boundary |P(H)-θ|≈0, small uncertainty can have large decision impact.
rationale_evidence.statement: Defines a decision boundary θ=0.8 and argues that near the boundary, small uncertainty in P(H) can have disproportionately large decision impact.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.42 — Why this matters ... If uncertainty is epistemic, MoreEvidence may reduce it. If uncertainty is intrinsic, MoreObservation may not eliminate the underlying variability.
rationale_evidence.statement: Explains the practical stakes of the aleatory/epistemic distinction: epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by more evidence, while aleatory/intrinsic uncertainty may not be eliminated by more observation.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.59 — Uncertainty should not silently accumulate ... If the system simply stores Confidence=0.9 at each stage, multiplying 0.9^4 would itself be unjustified. The semantics of the confidence measures must be known.
rationale_evidence.statement: Warns against naively multiplying stage-wise confidence scores (e.g. 0.9^4 across four pipeline stages) without knowing what each confidence measure actually means semantically.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 82.61 — False precision ... Input: 'roughly 80%' becoming Output: 0.813742. The mathematical formatting has become more precise than the underlying information.
rationale_evidence.statement: Illustrates false precision: a qualitative input ('roughly 80%') rendered as an overly precise numeric output (0.813742) misrepresents the underlying information's actual precision.

sources.note: S0919's Step 26: the formal model/reality projection gap, identifiability, and observability framework, directly extending S0918's (Step 25Z) M(W)!=W and Unknown-Unknowns opening question with a full mathematical treatment (sufficient statistics, latent variables, model misspecification, observability matrices).

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS never observes the whole world ... W\rightarrow O\rightarrow M(O) ... M(O)\neq W. That is unavoidable ... know precisely what the model represents, what it does not represent, and under which conditions its conclusions are valid
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS never observes the whole world, formalizing W->O->M(O) with M(O)≠W as unavoidable, reframing the goal from a perfect reality-copy to explicit knowledge of what the model represents/omits/when it's valid.

rows.anchor: \pi:W\rightarrow O ... W_1\neq W_2 while \pi(W_1)=\pi(W_2) ... one of the deepest sources of uncertainty
rows.statement: Formalizes observation as a projection pi:W->O, noting distinct world states can map to the same observation — 'one of the deepest sources of uncertainty.'

rows.anchor: W_1\sim_O W_2 if \pi(W_1)=\pi(W_2) ... Observationally indistinguishable\neq identical
rows.statement: Defines observational equivalence W1~_O W2, giving Observationally indistinguishable ≠ identical.

rows.anchor: CPU=40%, Memory=50%, HTTP=200 ... Reality A: Database healthy. Reality B: Database degraded but traffic is currently low ... O_A=O_B but W_A\neq W_B
rows.statement: Worked example: a healthy-database reality and a degraded-but-low-traffic reality produce identical monitoring observations.

rows.anchor: WorldState=Underdetermined ... another form of Zero. Not the system failed. Rather the available observations do not identify the relevant world state
rows.statement: Defines WorldState=Underdetermined as another form of Zero when multiple materially different states remain consistent with observations, explicitly not a system failure.

rows.anchor: X is identifiable from O if \pi(W_1)=\pi(W_2) always implies X(W_1)=X(W_2) ... X is not identifiable from the available observations
rows.statement: Formally defines identifiability of a property X from observations O.

rows.anchor: I am 95% confident ... structurally unidentifiable ... service returned HTTP 200 ... Is the database transaction durable? ... Confidence cannot compensate for missing information
rows.statement: Argues identifiability outranks confidence: a high-confidence AI claim can be unjustified if the property is structurally unidentifiable, worked with an HTTP-200/transaction-durability example — 'confidence cannot compensate for missing information.'

rows.anchor: RandomUncertainty from StructuralUncertainty. Random uncertainty may be reducible by more observations. Structural uncertainty may arise because the relevant variable is not observed at all. This is much more serious
rows.statement: Distinguishes random uncertainty (reducible by more observations) from structural uncertainty (unobserved relevant variable), the latter more serious.

rows.anchor: X\rightarrow Z\rightarrow Y ... EngineerExperience ... DeploymentMethod ... FailureRisk ... if we ignore experience, we may attribute the wrong causal effect to deployment
rows.statement: Worked latent-variable example: an unobserved EngineerExperience variable jointly driving deployment method and failure risk risks wrong causal attribution if ignored.

rows.anchor: Z\rightarrow X and Z\rightarrow Y ... observing X\leftrightarrow Y does not establish X\rightarrow Y ... reinforces the result from 25Z
rows.statement: Restates confounding: observed correlation does not establish causation, explicitly reinforcing the Step 25Z causal result.

rows.anchor: ModelBoundary ... variables represented; variables omitted; assumptions; applicable contexts; temporal validity; data sources; known limitations
rows.statement: Defines a required ModelBoundary specifying seven components a model must make explicit.

rows.anchor: ModelContract=(Inputs,Outputs,Assumptions,Scope,Validity,Limitations,Version) ... analogous to the ActionContract from 25Z
rows.statement: Defines a seven-field ModelContract explicitly analogous to the ActionContract from Step 25Z.

rows.anchor: NetworkLatency<100ms ... ModelApplicable\Rightarrow AssumptionsSatisfied. This should be a deterministic check where possible
rows.statement: Worked example: violating a model's stated assumption (network latency bound) invalidates applicability, giving ModelApplicable => AssumptionsSatisfied as a deterministic check.

rows.anchor: \mathcal D_{valid} ... outside it we should not silently extrapolate ... x\in[0,100] trained, x=500 received ... Computability\neq Validity
rows.statement: Defines a model validity region D_valid; a model can still compute an out-of-region output, but that does not establish validity — Computability ≠ Validity.

rows.anchor: CanCompute(x) from CanJustify(x) ... a model may technically compute f(x) while epistemically Justified(f(x))=False
rows.statement: States the profound distinction CanCompute(x) vs CanJustify(x): technical computability does not imply epistemic justification.

rows.anchor: ValidInference=Inference+ApplicabilityProof
rows.statement: Defines ValidInference as Inference plus an ApplicabilityProof spanning context/data/time/identity/semantics/model assumptions.

rows.anchor: T(E) ... P(E\mid T(E),\theta)=P(E\mid T(E)) ... sufficient statistic ... KnowledgeOS must be careful
rows.statement: Introduces the concept of a sufficient statistic T(E) retaining all information relevant to a parameter, with a caution against careless reliance.

rows.anchor: Mean=72 ... does not reveal outliers; multimodality; temporal structure; distribution shape ... SufficientFor(q_1)\not\Rightarrow SufficientFor(q_2)
rows.statement: Worked knowledge-compression example: a mean summary sufficient for one question can be insufficient for another (outliers/multimodality/temporal structure/shape hidden).

rows.anchor: Sufficient(E,q) ... a powerful safeguard against over-compression
rows.statement: Defines query-dependent sufficiency Sufficient(E,q) as a safeguard against over-compression.

rows.anchor: InformationLoss(T(E),q)>0 ... 4 million events summarized as daily average ... Safe for capacity trend. Unsafe for incident reconstruction
rows.statement: Defines InformationLoss(T(E),q) that the system should ideally record, worked with a large-event-set/daily-average example noting differing safety by use case.

rows.anchor: Summary\rightarrow SourceSet(E). Otherwise the summary becomes orphan knowledge
rows.statement: Requires compressed summaries to retain provenance to their source set, otherwise becoming orphan knowledge.

rows.anchor: Raw observation->Normalized observation->Evidence->Assertion->Domain concept->Knowledge->Decision ... every abstraction can discard information ... each transformation should have a semantic contract
rows.statement: Presents a seven-stage abstraction pipeline, each transformation potentially discarding information and requiring its own semantic contract.

rows.anchor: A:X\rightarrow Y ... InformationPreserved(A,q) ... conceptually explicit
rows.statement: Defines InformationPreserved(A,q) for an abstraction transformation, conceptually explicit even if not mathematically exact in every implementation.

rows.anchor: exact timestamp+IP+request ID -> service experienced high traffic ... Which customer caused the traffic spike? The abstraction cannot answer ... not a failure of inference. The information was discarded
rows.statement: Worked abstraction-leakage example: a downstream question the abstraction cannot answer reflects discarded information, not an inference failure.

rows.anchor: DerivedKnowledge must not replace underlying evidence ... Knowledge is a projection. The source evidence remains necessary for future questions
rows.statement: States the architectural principle that derived knowledge must not replace underlying evidence, since knowledge is a projection.

rows.anchor: Known, KnownUnknown, but there may also be UnknownUnknown ... cannot simply be placed into unknown=true because we do not know what it is
rows.statement: Defines Unknown Unknowns as relevant factors the current model does not even represent, explicitly not reducible to a simple unknown flag.

rows.anchor: repeated unexplained failures; systematic residuals; unexpected correlations; prediction failures; contradictory evidence; domain-expert objections; distribution shifts ... model adequacy signals
rows.statement: Lists seven model-adequacy signals indirectly detecting model incompleteness, since unknown unknowns cannot be computed directly.

rows.anchor: R=Y_{observed}-Y_{predicted} ... R\sim Time suggests temporal structure ... R\sim Environment suggests a missing environmental variable
rows.statement: Defines residual analysis R=Y_observed-Y_predicted, with structured residuals suggesting a missing variable.

rows.anchor: Y=f(X,Z) correct structure ... Y=f(X) misspecified ... No amount of parameter tuning necessarily fixes the missing Z
rows.statement: Defines model misspecification as a structural failure more serious than parameter error, since tuning cannot fix a missing variable.

rows.anchor: ModelCritique ... Where does it fail? Under what conditions? Which assumptions break? Which residual patterns exist? Which observations cannot be explained?
rows.statement: Defines a formal ModelCritique concept posing five diagnostic questions.

rows.anchor: A contradiction is not always bad data. It can be evidence that the model is incomplete ... Contradiction->DataError, ModelError, SemanticError, or IdentityError
rows.statement: Reframes contradiction as potentially model evidence, not merely bad data, with a four-way diagnostic split the system should distinguish.

rows.anchor: M_1,M_2,M_3 ... should not select purely on Fit. We also consider complexity; assumptions; generalization; causal plausibility; domain validity
rows.statement: States model selection among competing models should weigh five factors beyond mere fit.

rows.anchor: Simple\neq True ... simplicity is a model-selection principle, not an epistemic guarantee
rows.statement: States Occam's razor is a model-selection principle, not an epistemic guarantee — Simple ≠ True.

rows.anchor: P(Y\mid E)=\sum_i P(Y\mid E,M_i)P(M_i\mid E) ... captures model uncertainty ... not every KnowledgeOS decision needs Bayesian model averaging. The bounded context determines the appropriate machinery
rows.statement: Defines Bayesian model averaging as a way to capture model uncertainty, explicitly not required for every decision — the bounded context determines the appropriate machinery (RuleEngine vs ModelUncertainty).

rows.anchor: ModelMeaning(M,C) ... An Infrastructure model may be inappropriate for Architecture Governance ... ModelPortability requires ContextValidation
rows.statement: Defines ModelMeaning(M,C) as context-relative, giving ModelPortability requires ContextValidation, worked with cross-domain model-inapplicability examples.

rows.anchor: A system is observable when internal states can be inferred from available outputs sufficiently for the task ... Y_{0:T}\rightarrow X_T
rows.statement: Defines Observability formally: internal state reconstructable from observation history.

rows.anchor: Nexus: Version observable, Port 8081 observable, Internal cache observable? uncertain, Future failure not directly observable ... prevents the system from treating hidden state as known state
rows.statement: Worked example of per-property observability awareness, preventing hidden state from being treated as known state.

rows.anchor: \mathcal O=[C;CA;CA^2;\ldots;CA^{n-1}] ... rank(\mathcal O)=n ... full state is observable ... not impose this formalism on every KnowledgeOS component ... can the desired state actually be reconstructed from available observations?
rows.statement: Introduces the classical linear-systems observability matrix and full-rank condition as an analogy, explicitly not imposed on every component but valuable as a conceptual question.

rows.anchor: ObservabilityGap ... We need to know whether repository corruption occurred, but no integrity check exists ... not ask the LLM harder. It is: Add an observation mechanism
rows.statement: Defines ObservabilityGap with a worked example, stating the correct response is adding an observation mechanism, not prompting the LLM harder.

rows.anchor: AcquireObservation ... connects directly to 25Z's Value of Information ... run repository verification -> integrity confirmed
rows.statement: Connects observability-gap resolution to the Step 25Z Value-of-Information framework, worked with a repository-verification example.

rows.anchor: Observation(A) ... run health check; query CMDB; inspect deployment; verify certificate; check repository checksum ... InformationAcquisition can itself be an action
rows.statement: Restates active sensing: KnowledgeOS can actively request observations, five examples given, InformationAcquisition can itself be an action.

rows.anchor: ReadOnlyObservation from WorldChangingIntervention ... policy engine may prefer Observe before Act
rows.statement: Distinguishes ReadOnlyObservation from WorldChangingIntervention, with policy preferring observation before action given typically lower risk.

rows.anchor: Hypothesis\rightarrow ObservationRequest\rightarrow Observation\rightarrow HypothesisUpdate ... essentially scientific reasoning ... what information would distinguish competing hypotheses
rows.statement: Defines an active-diagnosis loop, described as essentially scientific reasoning.

rows.anchor: H_1:DatabaseFailure, H_2:NetworkFailure ... O^*=DatabaseConnectionTest ... P(O^*|H_1) and P(O^*|H_2) differ substantially ... a mathematically principled diagnostic action
rows.statement: Worked discriminating-observation example choosing a diagnostic test whose likelihood differs substantially under two competing hypotheses.

rows.anchor: IG(O)=H(\mathcal H\mid E)-H(\mathcal H\mid E,O) ... one rigorous way to choose the next diagnostic step
rows.statement: Defines an information-gain-based observation-selection criterion over a hypothesis space.

rows.anchor: IG(O) is not enough. We should consider VOI(O) ... decision impact; acquisition cost; risk
rows.statement: States information gain alone is insufficient for action selection; VOI(O) additionally weighs decision impact, cost, and risk.

rows.anchor: EpistemicPlanning=Choose the next observation/action that most improves the decision under constraints ... stronger than ordinary task planning
rows.statement: Defines EpistemicPlanning, stronger than ordinary task planning.

rows.anchor: Falsification tests A-G: identical observations from two world states->Identifiability=False PASS; out-of-domain input->Applicability=False/ExtrapolationWarning PASS; query-discarding summary->Sufficient(E,q)=False, retrieve underlying evidence PASS; strongly discriminating diagnostic observation pr
rows.statement: Runs seven falsification tests (A-G, all PASS) against the model-boundary/observability/identifiability model: two world states producing identical observations yield Identifiability=False without a forced claim of which state is true; an out-of-validated-domain model input yields Applicability=False or an ExtrapolationWarning; a query-discarding summary yields Sufficient(E,q)=False, prompting retrieval of underlying evidence; a strongly discriminating diagnostic observation may be preferred over immediate intervention between competing hypotheses; a model repeatedly failing under one environmental condition raises ModelCritique rather than merely lowering confidence; a hidden variable explaining contradictory observations becomes a candidate ModelExtension; and an LLM's precise answer despite structural non-identifiability yields Abstain/Underdetermined.

experiment.hypothesis: The model-boundary/observability/identifiability model behaves correctly across seven representative scenarios.
experiment.setup: Seven scenarios A-G spanning observational equivalence, out-of-domain extrapolation, over-compression, diagnostic observation selection, model critique triggers, hidden-variable model extension, and LLM overconfidence under non-identifiability.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the identifiability/applicability/sufficiency/model-critique rules to each scenario
experiment.result: All seven scenarios produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: Confirms the model prevents unjustified confidence and silent extrapolation.
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All seven tests PASS.

eq Reality ... Observation

rows.statement: Step 26 self-verdict: PASS, with six boxed non-equivalences headlined by Model≠Reality and Confidence≠Identifiability.

rows.anchor: I don't know [uncertainty] versus I cannot know this from the currently available observations [identifiability] ... That distinction is profound
rows.statement: States the profound safety-property distinction between a state of uncertainty ('I don't know') and a statement about identifiability ('I cannot know this from the currently available observations').

rows.anchor: Reality->Observation->Evidence->Representation->Model->Inference->Decision->Intervention ... each boundary needs its own contract ... ObservationContract, EvidenceContract, SemanticContract, InferenceContract, ModelContract, DecisionContract, ActionContract ... a very DDD-compatible architecture
rows.statement: Presents a consolidated eight-stage epistemic hierarchy with uncertainty/loss possibly introduced at every boundary, requiring seven named boundary contracts, each bounded context owning its meaning/invariants while KnowledgeOS provides shared epistemic infrastructure.

rows.anchor: Aleatoric, Epistemic, Model, Measurement, Semantic, Identity, Temporal, Causal ... Confidence=0.73 ... we lose critical information ... Step 27
rows.statement: Closes by listing eight distinct uncertainty kinds that collapsing into a single Confidence number would lose, transitioning to Step 27 (Uncertainty Calculus, Probability, Confidence, Belief, Evidence Weighting), posing the central question of representing uncertainty without turning every unknown into an arbitrary probability.
